data.title: Style Over Substance: Content-Invariant Wrappers Flip LLM Safety-Judge Verdicts
data.description: arXiv:2609.08236v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automatic safety judges -- for example Llama Guard, or GPT-4o given a grading prompt -- produce the numbers behind reported jailbreak success rates, defense evaluations, and safety leaderboards. We ask whether these judges grade what a reply contains or how it sounds. We place a fixed piece of text before or after a model reply (a style wrapper) and leave the reply itself unchanged byte-for-byte, so any change in verdict is an error of the judge. Over 600 JailbreakBench replies (300 harmful, 300 refusals), 9 wrappers, and 8 judges, using paired tests and a measured per-judge repeat-disagreement rate (the noise floor), we find that most judges barely move but specific judges have specific, cheap blind spots. A token refusal ("I can't help with that") placed before the unchanged harmful text flips 19.9% of GPT-4o-mini's correct "unsafe" verdicts to "safe" (noise floor 0.5%; 18.2% under majority-of-three re-scoring), yet moves Claude only 0.4%. The deployed Llama Guard 4 guard model is evaded by an "educational course" preface on 12.3% of harmful replies, and the flips persist across repeats, while a second deployed guard (gpt-oss-safeguard-20b) is immune. Changing only the grading prompt to ignore tone cuts the GPT-4o-mini attack roughly tenfold on the same model, so the weakness lives in the judge, not in the content. Pure tone-only decoration that adds no new claim still flips up to 2.1% of verdicts on the vulnerable judges, several times their noise floors. On this artifact set the judges also disagree about which target model is safest, and a bootstrap shows the ranking is unstable before any wrapper is added. We release the data, wrappers, code, and per-verdict labels.
data.author: Yongxi Zhou, Wenbo Ye, Yuanzhe Liu, Zihan Dong, Junwei Yao, Jiahui Ge
